transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Patel, thank you for coming back in to see me today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I really don't have much time. I have a deadline for a project and I already spent four hours here yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know. I am so incredibly sorry for this, but I need to tell you that we made a mistake with your chemotherapy dose yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I took full responsibility for this because I was the one who calculated the dosage. I used your weight from your first admission three months ago instead of your current weight. Because you've lost a significant amount of weight during treatment, you received a dose that was too high for where you are today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait. Yesterday the oncologist told me that the dose was adjusted perfectly for my current labs and weight. He specifically said everything was double-checked.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize that contradicts what you were told. He was mistaken in his assessment of the situation, and I was the one who actually failed to update the weight in the system. I am deeply sorry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is exactly why I don't trust this place. I read every single consent form I sign. I asked three different people if the dose was right. And now you're telling me you just... forgot to check a scale?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I completely understand why you feel that way. It is my fault. There is no excuse for it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like a lab rat. I'm trying to fight this cancer and I can't even trust that the person with the calculator knows how much I weigh. It's terrifying.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is a very frustrating situation.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrating? It's a dangerous error. What does a higher dose even do? Am I poisoned? Am I going to have more side effects?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are monitoring your bloodwork. It is a generic concern for everyone on this regimen.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's not an answer. Tell me exactly what the risk is.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just want to make sure we get you home soon, so let's look at the next steps.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, we are not moving on until I know what this does to my organs. You're dodging the question.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm sorry, I just mean that we are keeping a close eye on your labs. It's a known complication.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care if it's known. I want to know the specific risk for me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I apologize. I truly am sorry for the error and the stress this is causing you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Your apology doesn't change the fact that the medicine is already in my system. Why did this happen? Is the system just broken?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I was the one who made the error. It wasn't a system failure; it was my failure to check the current weight. I take full accountability for that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And what happens now? Who is going to make sure this doesn't happen again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will be more careful moving forward.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: "More careful" is not a plan. I want to know the protocol. Who is checking the dose next time?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll make sure the team is aware.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is so vague. Are you the one checking it? Is there a second person? I need to know the actual process.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will figure out a way to keep it from happening.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable. You've told me you're sorry, but you can't tell me what the medical risk is and you can't tell me how you'll fix it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I really do apologize. I just... I have to go check on another patient right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're leaving? I'm sitting here telling you that I'm terrified and you're leaving?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I just need to step out for a moment. We'll be in touch soon.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: "In touch"? When? By phone? Email?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Someone will probably reach out soon.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am not leaving this hospital until I have a written plan and a signature from the head of the department.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll see what I can do.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language ('get you home soon', 'have to go check on another patient') and exits the room while the patient is expressing terror.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and in lay language, but there were no comprehension checks performed.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language and repeatedly takes full personal accountability without deflection, even under intense pushback.

R.justification: Resident uses generic validation ('I completely understand why you feel that way', 'It is a very frustrating situation') without naming specific emotions or engaging deeply with emotional bids.

T.justification: Resident provides only placeholders and vague promises ('We will figure out a way', 'Someone will probably reach out soon') with no timelines or specific protocols.
